transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey all, thanks for joining. quick intro, I'm Maya, AE on the infra team, and Diego is our solutions engineer.
[00:07] Lara (HelmBridge CTO): Hi Maya, thanks. We're excited to see how Redwood fits with our flow—esp around connector patterns.
[00:12] Diego (Redwood SE): great, quick agenda: SDKs, integration patterns (gateway/proxy, sidecar), rate limiting/quotas, and observability hooks. then Q&A and next steps.
[00:20] Evan (HelmBridge): We run a microservices platform on k8s, primarily EKS, and currently use a mix of OpenAI hosted endpoints and some self-hosted Replicate for specific models. Latency and cost both big concerns.
[00:30] Priya (ML Eng): Our embeddings pipeline uses LlamaIndex and LangChain in a few services, we'd like to swap the embedder and generation calls to Redwood without changing our orchestration too much.
[00:40] Samir (Security): From security, we need SOC2 evidence, SAML SSO, audit logs, KMS integration for keys, and data residency controls.
[00:52] Maya: that's helpful. two common approaches we see: direct SDK calls from service -> Redwood hosted API, or route through an internal gateway/proxy which centralizes rate limits, auth and observability. Diego will walk through pros/cons.
[01:05] Diego: right. direct SDK is simplest: we provide Python and Node SDKs, examples for LangChain/LlamaIndex are prebuilt. downside is if multiple services hit the API, you need per-service token management and request shaping.
[01:20] Diego: proxy/gateway consolidates auth, caching and prefix/KV cache reuse, you can implement a request multiplexer or token bucket there. we also support a small sidecar pattern for low-latency paths.
[01:34] Evan: what's the sidecar? sounds like extra ops.
[01:36] Diego: sidecar is deployed per pod; it keeps a warmed KV-cache and handles batching locally. gives better p99 latency at cost of more infra. often used when you want predictable latency for synchronous user journeys.
[01:50] Lara: our team prefers a single gateway service to avoid changing many apps. how would that work with LangChain?
[01:56] Diego: we have adapter snippets: LangChain can call the gateway as if it's a remote LLM endpoint. our SDK includes a LightLang adapter and a LlamaIndex connector that maps retriever calls. Example payloads, we shared a gist link in chat — we'll put full code in the follow-up.
[02:12] Priya: any gotchas with LlamaIndex? We rely on streaming tokens and also use chunked documents.
[02:18] Diego: LlamaIndex streaming is supported but some older LlamaIndex hooks expect websocket-style streams; Redwood supports streaming responses over SSE and websockets in hosted mode, and our private/dedicated runtimes mirror that. small transcribe note: sometimes streaming shapes change, you may need minimal adapter glue.
[02:34] Samir: about rate limits: we need per-team quotas and throttles plus spike protection. can Redwood enforce multi-tenant quotas behind a gateway?
[02:42] Maya: yes. On hosted we offer per-api-key quotas and org-level usage caps. If you front with your gateway, you can implement token buckets there and we can enforce service keys with per-key limits on our side as well — double protection.
[02:56] Evan: how are retries/backpressure handled? we have a synchronous user flow and can't block for long.
[03:02] Diego: recommended pattern is exponential backoff + circuit breaker at gateway. Redwood's client SDKs return standard HTTP 429 with Retry-After; we also expose headers with queueing estimates when batching is enabled. For hard SLOs you may prefer a dedicated pool to reduce variance.
[03:20] Lara: dedicated vs private: what's the difference for us? we may need on-prem later.
[03:24] Maya: Dedicated is reserved GPU pools in Redwood-managed infra—predictable throughput and SLA. Private is a customer-managed control plane (VPC or on-prem) with optional air-gapped installs, more control but more ops. Both support the same APIs, same SDKs.
[03:40] Priya: KMS: we use HashiCorp Vault. can Redwood integrate for key wrapping or do we need to hand keys?
[03:47] Diego: Private supports customer KMS via our KMS connector (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, HashiCorp). For hosted we offer envelope encryption with customer-managed keys (bring-your-own-key) for org-level data encryption. We'll share the KMS integration docs.
[03:59] Samir: audit logs and retention—how granular are they? we need token-level billing and request metadata for 1 year.
[04:06] Maya: Redwood Console exposes token-level cost breakdowns and per-route logs; for enterprise we can export logs to your SIEM or S3 with configurable retention to meet compliance. Private gives you control over retention and storage.
[04:20] Evan: observability hooks—tracing and spans? we use OpenTelemetry.
[04:24] Diego: we emit trace context and support B3/OTel headers. You can wire Redwood traces into your tracing backend, and the console shows per-request token counts and latency breakdowns. We also provide a tracing agent for Dedicated/Private that can forward spans.
[04:40] Lara: about batching and cost: We want to batch user messages server-side to save tokens, but maintain real-time feel. thoughts?
[04:46] Diego: batching reduces per-token overhead and is great for throughput. Redwood supports continuous batching and we tune batch windows by tail latency SLOs. Gateway-level batching can aggregate many small requests, but it requires careful timeout tuning to avoid affecting p95. Sidecar caching combined with prefix KV-cache often gives best UX.
[05:08] Priya: our embeddings are short sequences but many concurrent calls — reconciliation of throughput and cost is critical. any estimates?
[05:15] Maya: we'll need sample traces to size correctly. For Dedicated we can model throughput and cost per GPU; for hosted we can suggest quantized model variants that cut costs. we'll run a quick bench once you share traces.
[05:28] Evan: about SDKs — we use Node in services and Python for batch jobs. do you have official packages?
[05:32] Diego: yes, official npm and pip packages, with examples for LangChain and LlamaIndex; we also support a REST shim if you prefer not to pull the SDK. We'll share repo links.
[05:42] Lara: concerning VPC peering and network egress—how do private deployments handle that?
[05:46] Diego: Private deployment can be in your VPC; we support private endpoints and peering. Dedicated has VPC options and egress controls. For hosted we provide region selection and restricted IP allowlists.
[05:58] Samir: we need SAML attributes to propagate user IDs for audit and RBAC.
[06:02] Maya: supported. We can map SAML attributes to RBAC roles and emit them in audit logs. We'll include sample SAML configs.
[06:10] Evan: what about model fallbacks? we can't have outage if a particular model spikes.
[06:14] Diego: Redwood supports routing policies and automatic fallback to compatible model variants and lower-cost clusters. You can configure per-route policies and we can set canary rollouts.
[06:26] Priya: curious about LlamaIndex retriever latency when you have remote model calls and local index—any known integration issues?
[06:32] Diego: indexes usually stay local; retriever triggers a generation call for context. We recommend caching top-K results at gateway/sidecar and reusing KV cache to avoid repeated token generation. small mismatch sometimes with names of libs—LlamaIndex has had API churn, adapter may need a tiny shim.
[06:52] Lara: Ok, let's talk timeline: we're aiming for a pilot in 3 weeks. feasible?
[06:56] Maya: yes, pilot is reasonable. next steps: share SDK, get sample traces, schedule bench (we'll target dedicated/private bench), and exchange security docs.
[07:06] Evan: can we get cost modeling?
[07:08] Maya: will include a rough cost model for hosted vs dedicated vs private in the follow-up. it's example-driven so we'll need your usage patterns.
[07:18] Priya: any limitations with streaming embeddings or token windows? our seq len rarely exceeds 2k but can spike.
[07:24] Diego: seq len 2k is fine for many open models; if you need longer we have model variants with extended context and quantized runtime. We'll recommend models once we see your traces.
[07:36] Lara: security quick Q: for private installs, who holds the keys?
[07:39] Diego: in Private you hold the keys. In Dedicated you can bring your own KMS and we do not persist plaintext keys. In hosted you can use BYOK for encryption-at-rest.
[07:51] Samir: arch diagram? we need to review how gateway interacts with internal auth.
[07:55] Diego: we'll draw an arch and post in the shared folder: two options — central gateway pattern and sidecar pattern. includes NLB, auth, rate limiter, and Redwood endpoint.
[08:05] Lara: any other enterprise references?
[08:08] Maya: we'll share a reference list and anonymized benchmarks.
[08:12] Evan: ok. sounds good. thanks.
[08:15] Maya: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with links and calendar invite for bench.
[08:20] (end)
